presidentialSuccession.name: Manuel Zelaya
presidentialSuccession.notes: Ousted in June 2009 coup; later founded LIBRE.

presidentialSuccession.name: Nasry Asfura
presidentialSuccession.notes: Declared winner of the 30 Nov 2025 election on 24 Dec 2025 by 0.74 points over Salvador Nasralla; both LIBRE and Nasralla's party challenged the results. Inaugurated 27 January 2026.

supremeCourt.name: Corte Suprema de Justicia
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Magistrates elected by the National Congress for 7-year terms.
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: Before the FSP era: in Dec 2012 Congress removed four Constitutional Chamber justices ("technical coup"), and in 2015 the court lifted the ban on presidential re-election (enabling Hernández). Under Castro/LIBRE, Congress elected a new 15-magistrate court in Feb 2023.
supremeCourt.stillServing: The 15-magistrate court elected by Congress in Feb 2023 (under LIBRE) is current; its partisan balance reflects the multi-party negotiation in Congress.

courtHistory.event: Through the 'banana republic' era and the military governments (1960s–80s) the court was weak; the 1982 Constitution set the current 15-magistrate court elected by Congress.
During the coup against President Zelaya, the Supreme Court ordered his arrest — pivotal, as Zelaya later founded the FSP-member party LIBRE.
In December Congress summarily removed four Constitutional Chamber justices (a 'technical coup') after rulings against the government.
The Supreme Court struck down the ban on presidential re-election, enabling Juan Orlando Hernández's 2017 re-election.
Under the Castro/LIBRE government, Congress elected a new 15-magistrate court in February after a multi-party negotiation.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: The 15-magistrate CSJ elected in 2023 is current; individual members are not itemized here.

benchControl.note: The 2016–2023 Supreme Court was elected in 2016 by a Congress controlled by the Hernández (Partido Nacional, non-FSP) government; LIBRE had no role in its selection. The 2012 removal of four Constitutional Chamber justices (the 'technical coup') and the 2015 ruling that lifted the presidential re-election ban both came from courts seated under non-FSP governments — the FSP party never controlled these benches.

In February 2023 the LIBRE-led Congress elected the 2023–2030 Supreme Court (the 15 magistrates require a two-thirds vote, from a list vetted by a nominating board). After three weeks of deadlock the seats were distributed by a negotiated tripartite pact — about 6 of the 15 magistrates were counted as LIBRE-aligned, 5 as Partido Nacional and 4 as Partido Liberal. It was LIBRE's largest-ever share of the bench but short of a majority; a PSH deputy criticised it as a new tripartite 'reparto'.

fspParties.note: LIBRE, formed in 2011 by supporters of the ousted Manuel Zelaya, is Honduras's FSP member. Before 2011 there was no FSP party in Congress.

legislativeControl.seats: LIBRE first contested Congress in 2013 as the main left opposition to the governing Partido Nacional.
With Xiomara Castro's 2021 win LIBRE became the largest bloc in Congress (about 50 of 128) but without a majority — it governs in alliance with Salvador Nasralla's PSH.

LIBRE returned to opposition under Asfura's PN government. In the CNE-certified 2026–2030 Congress the PN holds a plurality of 49 of 128, the Liberal Party 41 and LIBRE 35 (PINU-SD 2, DC 1) — no party has a majority.

government.note: The Partido Nacional's Nasry Asfura won the presidency and PN took a plurality of Congress (49 of 128); no party reached the 65-seat majority, so lawmaking depends on cross-party alliances. LIBRE, the FSP member, returned to opposition with 35 seats. The CNE issued its final declaration on 30 December 2025, having declared Asfura the presidential winner on 24 December with ~40.2% of the vote; both LIBRE and the Liberal Party's Salvador Nasralla disputed the count. PL and LIBRE are counted as opposition to the PN government but are ideological opposites and do not form a common bloc; PINU-SD (2) and the Christian Democrats (1) hold the balance.

LIBRE won a plurality (50/128); even with its electoral ally PSH (10) the government bloc held 60 seats — 5 short of a majority. The gap showed immediately: in January 2022 a group of LIBRE dissidents backed a rival congressional leadership, splitting the chamber before a negotiated settlement. Castro governed without reliable control of Congress.
